item.title: Private Equity: How It Works and What It Looks Like to an Investor
item.summary: Private equity means owning stakes in companies that are not listed on a public exchange, usually through a locked-up fund run by a specialist manager. It matters because these funds have unusual payoffs, fees, valuation methods and cash-flow patterns, and the exam expects you to recognise them.

sections.heading: What private equity is
sections.body_markdown:
**Private equity (PE)** is ownership in firms whose shares do not trade on a public exchange. Think of buying a share in a local family restaurant instead of a listed restaurant chain. You cannot sell it at a screen price on any given day, and the firm discloses far less information.

Most institutions invest through a **fund**. A specialist manager, the **general partner (GP)**, picks and manages the companies. The investors, the **limited partners (LPs)**, supply most of the money and have limited liability, so they can lose only what they put in. The typical goal is to buy into a private firm, improve it, and exit later through an IPO (listing on an exchange) or a sale to another company or investor.

sections.heading: Two main styles: venture capital and buyouts
sections.body_markdown:
**Venture capital (VC)** funds young, small firms. Early money often comes from founders and **angel investors** (friends, family and wealthy individuals). Institutions usually join at the **seed** stage and later rounds, ending with an exit. Each venture is like a lottery ticket: a high chance of losing most or all of the stake and a small chance of a huge payoff. VC investors also commonly help run the business.

A **buyout** takes an established company, often a listed one, into private ownership by buying a controlling or full equity stake. In a **leveraged buyout (LBO)** a PE firm or other outside investor funds the purchase with a large share of **debt**. The same idea applies to buying a house with a big mortgage: leverage magnifies gains and losses on the equity. Two variants differ by who leads the deal:

- **Management buyout (MBO):** the target's *existing* managers lead the purchase.
- **Management buy-in (MBI):** an *outside* management team leads the purchase.

Buyouts try to release value by cutting costs, selling poor or non-core assets, changing leverage, or replacing management.

sections.heading: Fund structure and fees
sections.body_markdown:
LPs make a **commitment** of capital, and the GP draws it down over time through **capital calls** as deals are found. Distributions come back as investments are exited.

The GP is paid in layers:

- A **management fee**, a percentage of committed or invested capital, paid whether or not the fund does well.
- **Carried interest (carry)**, a share of profits (20% is a common figure) paid as performance pay.
- Sometimes other fees, such as deal, advisory or directorship fees.

Two protections for LPs matter on the exam. A **hurdle rate (preferred return)** means carry is paid only on profits above a minimum return. A **clawback** lets LPs recover carry that was paid on early winners if later losses mean the GP ended up with more than its fair share over the whole fund life.

sections.heading: Illiquidity, valuation, the J-curve and IRR
sections.body_markdown:
PE is **illiquid**. Capital is locked up for years, and no daily market price exists. Valuations are infrequent and based on appraisals or models, so reported returns are less comparable with public assets.

Because cash flows come at irregular times, performance is usually reported with the **internal rate of return (IRR)**, the discount rate that sets the present value of all cash flows to zero. Funds also quote **MOIC**, total value divided by money invested. IRR depends on the *timing and size* of cash flows (it is cash-weighted), and it makes an implicit assumption about reinvesting interim cash flows. A strong-looking IRR or multiple can therefore hide a mediocre underlying return.

The **J-curve** is the typical shape of the fund's since-inception IRR over time. It dips below zero in the early years because fees and organisational costs are expensed straight away and failed investments are written down quickly. Winners are recognised only later, when they are exited. The IRR then climbs and, if the fund succeeds, ends positive. The dip reflects conservative accounting more than a true economic loss.

worked_example.problem: An LP invests 100 in a PE fund at time 0. The fund makes no interim distributions, and the LP receives 200 at the end of year 5 after the portfolio is exited. Find the MOIC and the annual IRR (round IRR to two decimals in percent).
steps: Lay out the cash flows: t0 = −100, t1 to t4 = 0, t5 = +200.
Calculator (TVM method): press 2ND CLR TVM, then N = 5, PV = −100, PMT = 0, FV = 200, then CPT I/Y.
Alternative (cash-flow method): CF, then 2ND CLR WORK, CF0 = −100 ENTER, ↓ C01 = 0 ENTER, F01 = 4 ENTER, ↓ C02 = 200 ENTER, then IRR CPT.

formulas.name: Internal rate of return
formulas.where: CF_t is the net cash flow to the investor at time t (contributions negative, distributions positive, final NAV counted at the end if still held); IRR is the discount rate that makes the sum zero; T is the last period.

formulas.name: Multiple on invested capital
formulas.where: Distributions are cash paid back to the investor; remaining value is the current valuation of unsold holdings; capital invested is money paid in. MOIC ignores timing.

exam_traps: Treating a management buy-in as the same as a management buyout: in an MBO the existing managers lead, in an MBI an outside team leads.
Reading the early negative IRR of the J-curve as proof the fund is a bad investment. It mostly reflects fees and fast write-downs of losers, with gains recognised later.
Mixing up hurdle rate and clawback: the hurdle is a minimum LP return before carry is paid, while the clawback returns excess carry to LPs after the fact.
Treating a high IRR or high MOIC as conclusive on its own. IRR is cash-weighted and depends on timing and reinvestment assumptions, and MOIC ignores timing entirely.
Assuming private equity is only equity. The category can include equity-like debt, but venture capital and LBOs are the two main equity forms.
builds_on: Time value of money and IRR

item.stem: A private equity firm acquires a listed company and takes it private. The acquisition is led by a management team from outside the target firm. This transaction is best described as a:

options.text: management buyout, led by the target's current managers
options.explanation: Confuses an MBO with an MBI. In an MBO the target's existing managers lead the purchase, but here the team is from outside.

options.text: leveraged buyout, defined by the use of a large share of debt
options.explanation: An LBO is defined by heavy debt financing and an outside investor acquirer. The stem identifies who leads the deal, not how it is financed, so this does not pin down the type.

options.text: management buy-in, led by an outside management team
options.explanation: Correct. A management buy-in is the case where the acquiring managers come from outside the company.

item.stem: An LP contributes 100 to a PE fund at time 0. There are no other cash flows until the end of year 4, when the LP receives 180. Using annual compounding, the fund's IRR is closest to (round to two decimals in percent):

options.explanation: Divides the total 80% gain by 4 years. This is a simple average that ignores compounding.
Uses five periods instead of four (1.8^(1/5) − 1), miscounting the time between the cash flows.

item.stem: A PE fund reports a negative since-inception IRR in its first few years, then the IRR rises and turns positive as holdings are sold. The main reason for the early negative IRR is that:

options.text: regulators require private companies to be marked down in the first years of a fund
options.explanation: No such rule exists. Early write-downs come from accounting conservatism and failed investments, not a regulatory markdown requirement.

options.text: fees and expenses are written off early and failed investments are recognised before gains from winners are realised
options.explanation: Correct. Early costs and quick recognition of losers push the IRR down, while profits from successful exits arrive later.

options.text: the hurdle rate is deducted from LP capital before any investments are made
options.explanation: Confuses the hurdle with a cost. The hurdle only sets the return level above which carry is charged, and nothing is deducted from capital up front.

item.stem: An LP pays 100 into a PE fund at time 0 and receives no distributions. At the end of year 2, the fund's reported net asset value for the LP's stake is 81, which is treated as the final value. Using annual compounding, the since-inception IRR is closest to (round to two decimals in percent):

options.explanation: Divides the total 19% loss by 2 years. This is a simple average that ignores compounding.
Reports the total loss over the whole period as if it were the annual rate, ignoring that it took two years.

item.stem: A PE fund pays carried interest only after LPs have received their capital back plus a preferred return. Later in the fund's life, the GP is found to have received more carry than the fund's overall results justify. Which statement about the clawback provision is correct?

options.text: It lets LPs recover excess carry already paid to the GP
options.explanation: Correct. A clawback lets LPs reclaim carry paid on early successes when later losses mean the GP was overpaid.

options.text: It lets the GP recover unpaid management fees from LPs if the fund underperforms
options.explanation: Reverses the direction of the clawback. It protects LPs against overpaid carry and does not let the GP recover fees.

options.text: It sets the minimum return LPs must receive before the GP earns any carry
options.explanation: Describes the hurdle rate (preferred return), not the clawback.

item.stem: An LP considers a PE fund commitment that is expected to require a single payment of 100 today and return 140 at the end of year 3, with no other cash flows. The LP's required return is 8% per year, compounded annually. The NPV of the investment is closest to (round to two decimals):

options.explanation: Adds up the cash flows without discounting (140 − 100), ignoring the time value of money.
Discounts the 140 for only two years (140/1.08^2 − 100), miscounting the timing.

item.stem: Which statement best describes the payoff profile of an individual venture capital investment in a young firm?

options.text: A high probability of losing most or all of the stake and a small probability of a very large gain
options.explanation: Correct. Each venture is like a lottery ticket, with most failing and a few producing very large payoffs.

options.text: Stable, predictable returns because the investee firms have long operating histories
options.explanation: Confuses venture capital with established, mature companies. VC targets small, undeveloped firms with high failure rates.

options.text: Returns driven mainly by using large amounts of debt to buy control of a mature company
options.explanation: Describes a leveraged buyout, not venture capital.

item.front: What is the difference between a management buyout (MBO) and a management buy-in (MBI)?
item.back: In an MBO the target firm's existing management leads the acquisition. In an MBI an outside management team leads it.

item.front: What is a hurdle rate (preferred return) in a PE fund?
item.back: A minimum return LPs must receive before the GP earns carried interest, so carry is charged only on profits above that level.
A clause letting LPs recover carried interest paid to the GP on early gains if later losses mean the GP received more than its fair share over the fund's life.

item.front: Why does a PE fund's since-inception IRR typically follow a J-curve?
item.back: Fees, expenses and write-downs of failed investments are recognised early, pushing the IRR negative. Gains from winning exits come later and lift it positive.

item.front: Why can IRR alone mislead when judging a PE fund?
item.back: IRR is cash-weighted and depends on the timing of flows and an implicit reinvestment assumption. A high IRR or MOIC can coexist with a mediocre underlying return, and reported values rely on infrequent appraisals.

warnings: 1/6 items have the longest option as the key
